abstract.p: Doxorubicin (DOX) remains one of the most effective chemotherapeutic agents for a variety of solid tumors and hematological malignancies. Nevertheless, its clinical utility is restricted by DOX-induced cardiotoxicity (DIC), primarily driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis. Baicalin (BAI), a natural compound with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer properties, has shown cardioprotective effects in DOX-treated animal cardiac models, but its impact on human cardiomyocytes remains unexplored. This study was designed to assess the cardioprotective effects of BAI against human cardiac DIC using induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs). hiPSC-CMs were pretreated with BAI and exposed to acute (1 µM for 24 h) and long-term (0.3 µM for 7d) DOX treatments, with or without different BAI concentrations (1 µM, 10 µM, and 25 µM). Multielectrode array (MEA) analysis, Tunel and cleaved-caspase 3 staining, reactive oxygen species (ROS) analysis, and sarcomere protein staining were performed to assess the effects of BAI on human DIC. BAI treatment alleviates DOX-induced cytotoxic injury, reducing apoptosis, oxidative stress, and preventing sarcomere disorganization. Moreover, BAI attenuated the long-term DOX-induced electrophysiological alterations, stabilizing field potential duration, beat rate, spike amplitude, and conduction velocity. These findings suggest the potential protective role of BAI against the DOX-induced human cardiac toxicity, supporting a potential clinical application in cancer patients.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Doxorubicin (DOX) is an anthracycline drug with strong therapeutic effects in the treatment of multiple cancers1. However, its clinical application is limited due to the DOX-induced cardiotoxicity (DIC) that impacts patient prognosis and survival2–5. Acute DOX cardiotoxicity manifests after a single treatment and is associated with transient electrophysiological abnormalities such as conduction alterations and arrhythmias, occurring from seconds up to 48 h post-administration6–8. Chronic DIC, associated with the cumulative lifetime dose, can lead to irreversible alterations such as chronic dilated cardiomyopathy with decreased left ventricular ejection fraction, occasionally resulting in fatal outcomes4,6. This form of DIC is difficult to predict and clinically manage because it may appear several years after treatment cessation9,10. Based on the increasing number of cancer survivors who have received DOX treatment, the study of DIC is of great interest, and currently, no suitable biomarkers to enable early detection or the development of effective treatment strategies are available11,12.

DIC is associated with oxidative stress, cardiomyocyte morphological changes, cell death, and apoptosis13–17. In particular, cardiomyocytes are very susceptible to DOX-induced oxidative damage due to their relatively lower level of antioxidant enzymes, and it has been hypothesized that alterations in membrane function, due to DOX-induced oxidative damage, may be responsible for many of the observed ECG changes17,18. Moreover, cardiomyocytes have a lower ability to regenerate, so they are potentially more susceptible to the long-term adverse effects of DOX17–19. DIC is also associated with alterations in the expression and organization of troponins and with direct myofibril damage and sarcomere disorganization15,16.

The DOX-induced molecular and structural alterations in the cardiac muscle could still occur in clinically asymptomatic patients, leading to a progressive weakening of the heart muscle, which may appear much later in life2–5. Management of DOX effects requires continuous monitoring and cardioprotective therapies based on antioxidant drugs or agents such as dexrazoxane, a ROS-reducing agent18–22. However, clinical practice guidelines support its use only in a specific subset of patients, excluding many others who might benefit from a novel therapeutic strategy that needs to be established21,22.

Several studies, in the last few years, have focused on natural compounds in preventing the adverse effects of DOX23. In particular, flavonoids belong to the polyphenol compounds extracted from several plant species and represent a class of molecules with antioxidant properties that could mitigate DIC23–26. Among these, Baicalin (BAI), a molecule extracted from S. baicalensis Georgi, is a natural bioactive compound with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer activities27–35. Different preclinical studies performed on animal models have provided evidence that baicalin could be a promising therapeutic agent for cardiovascular protection via inflammation regulation, inhibition of oxidative stress, and reduction of cardiomyocyte apoptosis36–39. However, there is no data regarding the cardioprotective effects of baicalin against the electrophysiological and structural DOX-induced damage in cardiac human models.

The human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) have revolutionized human cardiac disease and cardiotoxicity research, representing an in vitro human cardiac system for studying arrhythmia, cardiomyopathies, and to test cardiotoxicity both in short and long-term drug treatments40–45.

In this study, we use an integrated analytical approach combining cytotoxicity assays with hiPSC-CM–based multielectrode array (MEA) technology to investigate the structural and electrophysiological protective effects of BAI against acute and long-term DOX-induced cardiotoxicity. Our data revealed that Baicalin confers both structural and functional cardioprotection through multiple complementary mechanisms, including anti-apoptotic, antioxidant effects, structural preservation, and stabilization of electrophysiological activity of hiPSC-CMs. These results underscore the potential of BAI as a cardioprotective agent and provide a strong rationale for further translational research in the context of chemotherapy-associated cardiac risk.

sec.title: Baicalin reduced the DOX-induced apoptosis in hiPSC-CMs
sec.p: In humans, DOX can induce cell death of CMs, and it has also been demonstrated that it triggers apoptotic cell death in hiPSC-derived CMs14,41–43.

To evaluate the effect of BAI on DOX-induced cytotoxicity, we performed a cell viability assay after acute (1 µM DOX, 24 h) and long-term (0.3 µM DOX, 7d) DOX treatments, with or without different BAI doses (1 µM, 10 µM, and 25 µM). Compared with control cells, DOX exposure markedly reduced cell monolayer viability and density, as indicated by a significant decrease in the Calcein-positive area following acute (59%±3% vs. 84%±1.6%, p < 0.0001) and long-term (65%±1.8% vs. 81%±1.4%, p < 0.0001) DOX treatments (Fig. 1a and b). BAI co-treatment counteracted DOX-induced cell death, leading to a significant increase in the Calcein-positive area, particularly in cells treated with 10 µM and 25 µM BAI, in both acute (80%±1.7% and 74%±1.6%, respectively; p < 0.0001) and long-term DOX conditions (78%±2% and 79%±1.2%, respectively; p < 0.0001) (Fig. 1a and b). Consistently, a significant reduction in EthD-1-positive dead cells was observed in BAI-treated cultures under both acute and long-term DOX exposure (Supplementary Fig. 1), confirming the effects observed with calcein staining. Long-term DOX treated hiPSC-CMs showed a more shaped morphology compared with the acute ones (Fig. 1a and b). Therefore, the reduced Calcein-positive area observed in these cardiomyocytes is not entirely associated with cell damage or death, as further confirmed by the EthD-1 analysis (Supplementary Fig. 1b).

caption.p: Cell viability assays in acute and long-term DOX treated hiPSC-CMs. (a) Immunofluorescence staining (left panel) of green Calcein (live) positive hiPSC-CMs treated with DOX 1 µM for 24 h with or without BAI at the indicated doses; quantitative analysis of viability expressed as calcein positive area / total area (right panel). (b) Immunofluorescence staining (left panel) of green Calcein (live) positive hiPSC-CMs treated with DOX 0.3 µM for 7 days, with or without BAI at the indicated doses; quantitative analysis of viability expressed as Calcein positive area / total area (right panel). Data are presented in box plots indicating median (middle line), 25th, 75th percentile (box), and min and max data points (whiskers). n = 12 replicates/group from 3 independent experiments. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s post hoc test: ****p < 0.0001. Phase contrast 60X. Scale bar: 50 μm.

sec.p: Taken together, our results indicate that BAI at 10 µM and 25 µM significantly preserved hiPSC-CM viability, mitigating DOX-induced cell death under both treatment conditions (Fig. 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1).

We therefore assess whether BAI improves DOX-induced apoptotic cell death in hiPSC-CMs by performing Tunel assay and cleaved Caspase-3 immunostaining under the same experimental conditions. After acute DOX exposure, a higher apoptotic rate was detected in DOX-treated hiPSC-CMs compared with control cells (25.2%±2.6% vs. 1.4%±0.1%, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 2a). BAI co-treatment contrasts with the DOX-induced cell death, showing a significant decrease in the apoptotic rate, particularly in cells treated with DOX 1 µM plus BAI 10 µM (2.9%±0.3%, p < 0.0001) and DOX 1 µM plus BAI 25 µM (4.3%±0.6%, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 2a).

caption.p: BAI contrasts the acute and long-term DOX-induced apoptosis in hiPSC-CMs in a dose-dependent manner. (a) and (c) Immunofluorescence staining (left panel) and quantitative analysis (right panel) of Tunel-positive cardiomyocytes in acute (a) and long-term (c), DOX and BAI co-treated hiPSC-CMs. (b) and (d) Immunofluorescence staining (left panel) and quantitative analysis (right panel) of cleaved Caspase-3 positive cells in acute (b) and long-term (d) DOX and BAI co-treated hiPSC-CMs. Data are presented in box plots indicating median (middle line), 25th, 75th percentile (box), and min and max data points (whiskers). n = 9 replicates/group from 3 independent experiments. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s post hoc test: **p < 0.01 and ****p < 0.0001. Phase contrast 60X. Scale bar: 50 μm.

sec.p: Consistent with Tunel results, a high percentage of cleaved Caspase-3 positive cells was observed in DOX 1 µM treated hiPSC-CMs, compared with control (21.3%±1.3% vs. 1.0%±0.5%, p < 0.0001) and with BAI 10 µM (2.5%±0.7%, p < 0.0001) and BAI 25 µM (1.8%±0.6%, p < 0.0001) co-treated cells (Fig. 2b). These results demonstrate a protective role of BAI against acute DOX-induced apoptosis in hiPSC-CM.

We further assess the effect of BAI on long-term DOX toxicity. A higher apoptotic rate was detected in DOX-treated cells compared with control hiPSC-CMs (17%±1.4% vs. 1.7%±0.3%, p < 0.0001). Similar to acute treatment, BAI exerted a protective effect against DOX-induced apoptosis also in the long-term treatment in a dose-dependent mode (BAI 1 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 8.5%±1.3%, p < 0.0001, BAI 10 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 2%±0.7%, p < 0.0001, and BAI 25 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 2.5%±0.2%, p < 0.0001) (Fig. 2c).

The analysis of cleaved Caspase-3 confirms the significant reduction in the percentage of cleaved Caspase-3 positive cells in BAI cotreated cells, compared with DOX 0.3 µM (BAI 1 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 9.3%±0.8%, p < 0.01, BAI 10 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 3.4%±0.7%, p < 0.0001 and BAI 25 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 2.5%±0.2%, p < 0.0001 vs. DOX 0.3 µM 13.1%±0.8% ) (Fig. 2d).
No effect on apoptosis was observed in the long-term exposure to BAI alone at all concentrations tested, indicating the safety of the compound in this human cardiac cell model (Supplementary Fig. 2).
Altogether, these data suggest that BAI significantly contrasts cell death and apoptosis in DOX-treated human cardiac models both in acute and long-term exposure.

sec.title: Baicalin contrasts DOX-induced oxidative stress in hiPSC-CM
sec.p: Oxidative stress is widely accepted as a key factor of DOX-induced cell death and cardiotoxicity8,12–14. To assess if the observed BAI protective effect against DOX-induced apoptosis is associated with the reduction of oxidative stress, we performed reactive oxygen species (ROS) analysis in hiPSC-CMs exposed to DOX and co-treated with BAI at different doses.

Compared with control cells, acute DOX exposure induced a significant increase of ROS (58%±3.2% vs. 0.2%±0.1%, p < 0.0001), detected as a green signal by the fluorogenic CellRox probe, primarily localized in the nucleus of cells (Fig. 3a). The BAI co-treatment significantly reduced ROS production, in particular the dose of 10 µM (26%±3.6%, p < 0.0001) and 25 µM (3%±0.6% p < 0.0001), while no significant reduction in ROS level was observed in BAI 1 µM co-treated cells (45%±3.6%, p > 0.01) (Fig. 3a).

caption.p: BAI contrasts the DOX-induced ROS production in hiPSC-CMs. (a) Representative fluorescent microscopy images (left panel) and quantification (right panel) of CellRox positive hiPSC-CMs treated with DOX 1 µM and BAI at the indicated doses. (b) Representative fluorescent microscopy images (left panel) and quantification (right panel) of CellRox positive hiPSC-CMs treated with long-term DOX 0.3 µM and BAI at the indicated doses. Data are presented in box plots indicating median (middle line), 25th, 75th percentile (box), and min and max data points (whiskers). n = 9 replicates/group from 3 independent experiments conducted in triplicate. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s post hoc test: **p < 0.01 and ****p < 0.0001. Phase contrast 60X. Scale bar: 20 μm.

sec.p: It is noteworthy that the nearly 50% reduction in ROS observed in Fig. 3a with BAI at 10 µM corresponds to a significantly greater reduction in apoptosis (Fig. 2a and b). To assess whether BAI affects DNA damage more than oxidative stress in response to DOX treatment, we performed γH2AX immunofluorescence staining after 24 h of DOX exposure, both with and without BAI. The results show that BAI reduces the formation of γH2AX nuclear foci, indicating protection against DOX-induced DNA damage and corroborating the Tunel assay findings reported previously (Supplementary Fig. 3).

We also analyzed oxidative stress in long-term DOX-treated cells, in the presence of BAI at different doses. After DOX treatment, punctate CellRox-positive spots were observed compared with control (11%±1.5% vs. 1%±0.2%, p < 0.0001). Co-treatment with BAI at 1, 10 and 25 µM significantly reduced this DOX-induced ROS accumulation (BAI 1 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 6.5 ± 0.6% p < 0.01, BAI 10 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 2%±0.2% p < 0.0001, and BAI 25 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 1%±0.5% p < 0.0001) (Fig. 3b).
These data demonstrated the protective role of BAI against DOX-induced oxidative stress in a human cardiac cell model, both in acute and long-term exposure.

sec.title: Baicalin prevented the long-term DOX-induced sarcomere disorganization in hiPSC-CM
sec.p: A hallmark of delayed DOX-induced cardiotoxicity is the morphological changes related to the myofibril damage and sarcomere disorganization, which impair their contractile capacity15,16. In order to study the role of BAI against long-term DOX-induced cardiac structural changes, we analyzed the sarcomeric proteins α-actinin (α-act) and cardiac troponin T (cTnT) in hiPSC-CMs after 0.3 µM DOX exposure with or without BAI at different doses.

The structural and sarcomeric regularity was visibly impaired after DOX exposure, compared with control hiPSC-CMs (Fig. 4a and b). In particular, punctate actinin staining, irregular myofibril structure, and loss of regular α-actinin banding were observed in DOX-treated cells (Fig. 4a and b). The co-treatment with BAI 10 µM and 25 µM significantly contrasted the DOX-induced sarcomere disarray (BAI 10 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 7.2%±0.9%, p < 0.0001 and BAI 25 µM plus DOX 0.3 µM 6.0%±1.7%, p < 0.0001 vs. DOX 0.3 µM 88.4%±2.7%), maintaining striated and compact sarcomere morphology with regular cTnT and α-actinin organization (Fig. 4a-c).

caption.p: BAI prevented the long-term DOX-induced sarcomere disorganization in hiPSC-CMs. (a) Immunofluorescence staining of α-actinin (α-act) and c-Tnt protein in DOX 0.3 µM and DOX 0.3 µM plus BAI-treated hiPSC-CMs. (b) Representative fluorescence intensity profile of α-actinin banding showing sarcomere irregularity in cells treated with DOX 0.3 µM. (c) Quantification of sarcomere disarray expressed as % of cells with α-actinin disorganization/total number of cells. The extent of α-actinin disorganization was evaluated in a blinded fashion by two independent observers on at least 50 cells per condition. Data are presented in box plots indicating median (middle line), 25th, 75th percentile (box), and min and max data points (whiskers). n = 12 replicates/group from 3 independent experiments. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s post hoc test: ****p < 0.0001. Phase contrast 100X. Scale bar: 10 μm.

sec.p: These data demonstrated a protective role of BAI at high doses against the structural cardiomyocyte damage associated with the long-term DOX-induced cardiotoxicity.

sec.title: Baicalin inhibits the long-term DOX-induced alteration of electrophysiological parameters in hiPSC-CMs
sec.p: It has been demonstrated that DOX treatment alters the electrophysiological properties of hiPSC-CMs with both acute and chronic effects41–45. To investigate the putative protective role of BAI on the DOX-induced electrophysiological alterations, we performed multi-electrode array (MEA) analysis in hiPSC-CMs after DOX acute and long-term treatment in the presence of different BAI doses.

The DOX 1 µM treatment induced waveform alterations starting from 12 h, with the stop of spontaneous beating (quiescence, Q) at 24 h post-treatment (Fig. 5a). However, these alterations are related to the cytotoxic effect of acute DOX exposure as demonstrated with impedance assay performed on the same samples (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Interestingly, BAI 10 µM and 25 µM co-treatment were able to mitigate these alterations (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 4a), confirming the protective role of BAI against DOX-induced cell death (Supplementary Fig. 1a and Fig. 2a).

caption.p: MEA signals recorded in DOX-treated hiPSC-CMs. (a) Representative waveforms recorded at 6 h, 12 h, 18 h, and 24 h from hiPSC-CMs monolayers on MEAs and subjected to DOX 1 µM and BAI at the indicated doses. (b) Representative waveforms recorded at 1d, 3d, 5d and 7d from hiPSC-CMs monolayers on MEAs and subjected to DOX 0,3 µM and DOX 0,3 µM plus BAI at different doses (1 µM, 10 µM, and 25 µM). The line in the waveform identifies the T wave peak, used to evaluate the FPD (the interval from the top of the spike to the peak of the “T-wave-like” repolarization waveform). F= flat T wave; Q= quiescence.

sec.p: A marked protective electrophysiological effect of BAI was observed in the long-term DOX treatment. Prolonged exposure to DOX 0.3 µM induced notable waveform alterations starting from 72 h of treatment, but in the absence of cell death (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 4b). Moreover, in agreement with previous studies, low DOX dose treatment in iPSC-CMs induced significant alterations in multiple MEA parameters41. In particular, after 72 h of DOX 0.3 µM exposure, iPSC-CMs exhibited a marked reduction in corrected Field Potential Duration (FPDc) (-26.8% ± 3.5% vs. 3.6% ± 1.7%, p < 0.0001), Beat Period (BP) (-21% ± 4% vs. 9.4% ± 5.2%, p < 0.001), Spike Amplitude (-73.9% ± 3.4% vs. -15.8% ± 5.5%, p < 0.0001), and Conduction Velocity (0.13 mm/ms ± 0.01 mm/ms vs. 0.24 mm/ms ± 0.01 mm/ms, p < 0.0001), when compared to vehicle-treated control cells (Fig. 6, a-e). The co-treatment with BAI at 10 µM and 25 µM significantly reduces these alterations. In particular, treatment with BAI 10 µM attenuated the reduction in FPDc (-4.5% ± 2.2%, p < 0.0001), BP (1.5% ± 4.9%, p < 0.001), Conduction Velocity (0.2 mm/ms ± 0.01 mm/ms, p < 0.001), and improved Spike Amplitude (-52.7% ± 3.3%, p < 0.01). Similarly, BAI 25 µM co-treatment resulted in significant protection of FPDc (-1.8% ± 2.4%, p < 0.0001), BP (8.6% ± 6.1%, p < 0.001), Conduction Velocity (0.2 mm/ms ± 0.01 mm/ms, p < 0.001), and Spike Amplitude (-49.9% ± 4.3%, p < 0.01) (Figs. 6, a-e).

caption.p: MEA analysis in DOX 0.3 µM-treated hiPSC-CMs. Measurement of FPDc (a), BP (b), Spike Amplitude (c), Conduction Velocity (e), and APD90 (g) across hiPSC-CMs monolayers on MEA after 3d of DOX 0.3 µM and BAI at the indicated doses. (d) Representative heatmaps of field potential (FP) propagation. The color scale indicates the time at which the sodium peak of the FP signal propagates from the start time (0 ms) to the end points (10 ms). (f) Representative spontaneous action potential (AP) traces from the indicated groups acquired after LEAP induction. Data are presented in box plots indicating median (middle line), 25th, 75th percentile (box), and min and max data points (whiskers). For FP analysis n = 20 replicates/group from 5 independent experiments conducted in quadruplicate. For LEAP analysis n = 8 replicates/group from 2 independent experiments conducted in quadruplicate. Statistical analysis was performed using two-way ANOVA and Tukey’s post hoc test; **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.0001, and ****p < 0.0001.

sec.p: To confirm the effect of BAI on FPDc reduction induced by DOX-treatment, we perform Action Potential Duration (APD) analysis. As reported in Fig. 6, panels f and g, DOX 0.3 µM induces a significant reduction of APD 90% (APD90) compared with control cells (0.5 s ± 0.004 s vs. 0.7 s ± 0.01 s, p < 0.0001). In agreement with FPDc results, BAI 10 µM and 25 µM significantly contrast DOX-induced APD90 reduction (0.6 s ± 0.01 s, p < 0.01 and vs. 0.6 s ± 0.01 s, p < 0.01, respectively).

Collectively, these data indicate a protective role of BAI 10 µM and 25 µM against the electrophysiological effects of long-term DOX exposure of hPSC-CMs, stabilizing FPDc, APD, beat rate, spike amplitude, and conduction velocity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the current study, we demonstrated the protective effects of BAI, a natural flavonoid with antioxidant, anti-apoptotic, and anticancer activities, against DOX-induced cardiotoxicity in a representative human cardiac model.

A hallmark of DOX-induced cardiac injury is the induction of cardiomyocyte death, and the apoptotic pathway is one of the most well-characterized programmed cell death pathways involved in DIC, as demonstrated in both in vivo and in vitro cardiac models12,13. Consistent with this, our results show that both acute and long-term DOX treatments induced a significant decrease in viability and an increase in apoptotic cell death in hiPSC-CMs. Moreover, a significant increase in intracellular ROS levels was observed in DOX-treated hiPSC-CMs, in line with previous studies17–20. In particular, in our experimental conditions, a nuclear CellRox signal was observed after DOX 1 µM for 24 h, consistent with acute oxidative and genotoxic stress, which is further supported by the concomitant increase in nuclear γ-H2AX foci, indicating DNA double-strand break formation under high-dose, short-term DOX exposure. Interestingly, our study indicates that BAI can contrast all these DOX cytotoxic effects both in acute and long-term treatments, with a marked protective effect obtained with BAI 10 µM and 25 µM doses. These results suggest a potent anti-apoptotic and antioxidative BAI activity in our human in vitro model, in agreement with previous data reported in cardiac animal models27–39,46.

Oxidative stress is widely accepted as a key factor of DOX-induced apoptosis8,12–14. Notably, BAI at 10 µM markedly reduced acute DOX-induced cell death and apoptosis, despite only a moderate decrease in total ROS levels. In addition, long-term exposure to 0.3 µM DOX induced significant cell death and apoptosis, despite relatively low ROS levels production, probably reflecting a chronic sublethal stress rather than the acute oxidative overload observed at higher DOX concentrations. These findings suggest that the anti-apoptotic effect of BAI may be mediated not only by attenuation of DOX-induced ROS production, but also by additional mechanisms, potentially including the preservation of DNA integrity, as reported in previous studies47,48. According to this hypothesis, the analysis of the effects of BAI on DNA integrity by immunofluorescence staining of γH2AX-positive cardiomyocytes demonstrated that BAI significantly inhibits DOX-induced genotoxic stress.

DOX-induced oxidative stress and apoptosis in hiPSC-CMs ultimately impair their structural integrity and function. Previous studies have shown that even low therapeutic DOX doses (< 0.5 µM) can markedly alter the cardiac sarcomeric organization, a key factor in maintaining normal contractility and myocardial function, and may contribute to the delayed malfunctioning of human cardiomyocytes of chronic DIC15,16,43. In line with this evidence, the long-term DOX treatment induced a marked sarcomeric disarray in iPSC-CMs. Interestingly, BAI 10 µM and 25 µM co-treatment was able to significantly preserve the α-actinin and troponin organization, suggesting a protective role of this natural compound against the cardiac structural alterations associated with the DOX-induced delayed cardiotoxicity.

In addition to its cytotoxic effects, DOX has also been associated with several functional alterations in humans, including arrhythmias, sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, T wave flattening, abnormalities of the QT interval, and atrio-ventricular nodal block2–5. Consistent with these clinical observations, in vitro studies indicated that DOX alters the electrophysiological properties of hiPSC-CMs with both acute and long-term effects on electrophysiological parameters, and the DOX-induced adverse effects on cardiac function can be detected in real-time with the MEA system41–45,49,50. These alterations include the modulation of corrected field potential duration, beat period, conduction velocity, and spike amplitude, and are correlated to a doxorubicin-induced cytotoxicity41–45,49,50. In the present study, for the first time, we demonstrate that BAI is able to improve the DOX-induced electrophysiological alterations in a human cardiac model. In particular, a marked BAI protective effect was observed against the DOX-induced reduction of FPDc, BP, Spike Amplitude, Conduction Velocity, and APD90, after 3 days of DOX 0.3 μM exposure. These results are not associated with iPSC-CMs cell death or detachment, as demonstrated by the simultaneous viability evaluation performed with the impedance assay.

All these parameters are commonly altered in models of DOX-induced cardiotoxicity, and this is associated with ROS overproduction, cytoskeletal disorganization, and sarcomeric disarray, all of which compromise myocardial architecture and function, increasing the arrhythmic risk and contractile dysfunction41–43,51–56. In our experimental conditions, despite the onset of electrophysiological changes recorded after long-term DOX exposure, no detachment or cell death was observed. Therefore, we could not exclude that other mechanisms involving the regulation of ion channels could be associated to the long-term DOX-mediated alteration of iPSC-CMs electrophysiology. However, the stabilization obtained with BAI co-treatment suggests a functional benefit associated with either the maintenance of cardiomyocyte structural integrity or the improvement of cardiomyocyte excitability and conduction.

Our results suggest that BAI may represent a novel cardioprotective agent in the human heart, able to avoid the acute and delayed DIC. Notably, the most protective effects of BAI were observed at concentrations of 10 µM and 25 µM. These doses were selected for their anticancer properties demonstrated in several human cancer cell models25–33. Therefore, the potential therapeutic use of BAI together with DOX could not only mitigate DIC but also improve drug anticancer activity.

Despite the promising findings, our study has some limitations. The hiPSC-CMs provide a relevant human-based model for studying DOX cardiotoxicity. However, they do not fully recapitulate the complexity of the adult human heart. Therefore, to confirm BAI efficacy and safety in a more complex physiological environment, further validation in preclinical and clinical studies is required. Another limitation of our study is the use of a single hiPSC line (iCell-CMs). Although this model is widely adopted for preclinical cardiotoxicity testing, the intrinsic variability between lines underscores the need for validation in additional hiPSC-CM models, in particular for the electrophysiological analysis. For instance, the FPDc reduction observed after DOX exposure in our study is consistent with previous findings in iCell-CMs, whereas other cardiac models have reported FPDc prolongation41–45,57. Moreover, several clinical studies have reported a prolongation of the QT interval in patients treated with DOX2–7. These discrepancies likely reflect limitations of hiPSC-CM models, which may arise from factors such as the absence of innervation, differences in cell composition (e.g., the proportion of ventricular, atrial, and nodal cardiomyocytes), variations in maturation, ion channel expression, and drug exposure. To enhance reproducibility and translational relevance, future studies should incorporate multiple cell lines from diverse donors or disease backgrounds, as well as utilize cardiac organoids.

Moreover, although BAI exerted strong protective effects at 10 and 25 µM in hiPSC-CMs, it should be noted that these concentrations are relatively high, and BAI is characterized by limited bioavailability, and these concentrations are pharmacologically challenging, potentially restricting its translational application58,59. Therefore, further preclinical studies will be necessary to optimize new strategies for formulation (e.g., nanoparticle encapsulation, prodrugs, structural analogs), delivery, and the development of derivatives with improved pharmacokinetic properties before considering clinical applications.

Finally, although our results demonstrated cardioprotective BAI effects in a human cardiac model against oxidative stress, apoptosis, sarcomere disorganization, and electrophysiological alterations, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these effects require further investigation. In particular, additional experiments will be necessary to clarify this finding and to determine whether BAI’s protective effect is primarily associated with the prevention of DOX uptake into cardiomyocytes or instead with the modulation of downstream stress pathways.

In conclusion, integrating hiPSC-CM-based MEA technology with cytotoxicity assays enabled the detection of both cardiotoxic and cardioprotective effects, reinforcing the value of human in vitro cardiac models for evaluating drug-induced cardiotoxicity and identifying novel protective compounds. This combined analytical approach revealed that baicalin confers both structural and functional cardioprotection of a human cardiac cell model, likely through multiple complementary mechanisms, including anti-apoptotic, antioxidant effects, structural preservation, and stabilization of electrophysiological activity. Overall, our findings highlight the effectiveness of Baicalin, particularly at 10 µM and 25 µM concentrations, in mitigating doxorubicin-induced cardiac damage, supporting its potential translational value as a promising cardioprotective agent during chemotherapy.

sec.title: Reagent
sec.p: Baicalin (sc-204638B, Santa Cruz) was dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) to prepare a 50mM stock solution, stored at − 80 °C. Doxorubicin was obtained from Sigma (D1515), and a 10mM stock solution was prepared in ddH2O. Toxic (1 µM) and therapeutic (0.3 µM) DOX working solutions were used to study acute and long-term DOX effects. Mouse monoclonal antibody α-actinin was purchased from Sigma (A7811), rabbit polyclonal cTnT was obtained from Abcam (ab45932), rabbit polyclonal cleaved Caspase-3 (D-175) and mouse monoclonal pH2AX (D7T2V) from Cell Signaling. Secondary antibodies anti-mouse and anti-rabbit IgG were obtained from Santa Cruz Biotechnology.

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: A commercially available line of human hiPSC-CMs, iCell-Cardiomyocytes (iCell-CM 01434, Lot numbers 106882), was purchased from Fujifilm Cellular Dynamics Inc. (Madison, WI, United States). Cells were seeded according to the instructions of the cell provider. A density of 2 × 104cells/well was used for electrophysiological studies on 48-well MEA plates (Axion Cytoview Plates, M768-tMEA-48B for Field Potential analysis and Axion Biocircuit Plates, M768-BIO-48 for Local Extracellular Action Potential (LEAP) analysis), while 1 × 104 cells/well was used for apoptotic, ROS analysis, and immunofluorescence assays on 15-well µ-slide (Ibidi). The maturation of the cardiomyocytes was obtained by maintaining plated cells in Culture Maintenance Medium (CMM, M1003, Cellular Dynamics) for four weeks, as previously described60,61.

sec.title: Experimental scheme
sec.p: After four weeks of maturation, iCell-CMs were exchanged with fresh CMM for 3 h and then were pre-treated with BAI at different concentrations (1, 10, and 25 µM) for 48 h. For acute treatment, the cardiotoxic dose of DOX 1 µM was used alone or in combination with BAI for 24 h. For long-term analysis, cells were treated for 7 days with DOX 0.3 µM in the presence of different BAI doses, with a media treatment refresh after 4 days. Cells treated with vehicles (H2O and DMSO 0.05%) were used as a control.

sec.title: Cell viability and apoptotic assays
sec.p: Cell viability was analyzed using the LIVE/DEAD™ Viability/Cytotoxicity Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.). The cell viability was estimated after live staining as the ratio of green Calcein-AM positive area/total area. Cell-death analysis was performed on samples fixed immediately after Calcein-AM/Eth-D1 live staining, and expressed as the ratio of Eth-D1–positive cells/number of Hoechst-positive nuclei.

Apoptotic cells were determined by the terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated dUTP nick end labeling assay (TUNEL assay, Promega) as well as by the analysis of cleaved Caspase-3 using immunofluorescence staining. Cells were nuclear-stained with Hoechst 33258 (Sigma-Aldrich). The apoptotic rate was estimated by the ratio of Tunel-positive nuclei/total nuclei.
For each analysis, at least three experiments were performed (n = 12 for cell viability test; n = 9 for Tunel and cleaved Caspase-3 analyses).

sec.title: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) detection
sec.p: Oxidative stress induced by reactive oxygen species (ROS) was measured using CellROX® Green Reagent (Life Technologies), according to manufacturer instructions. Upon oxidation, the CellROX® fluorophore becomes DNA-binding and fluoresces, producing a signal that is predominantly localized to the nuclei and mitochondria. After the previously described treatments, cells were incubated for 30 min at 37℃ with CellROX® reagent at a concentration of 5 µM. After washing in PBS, cells were fixed with 4% PFA and nuclei stained with Hoechst 33358. CellRox intensity was estimated by the ratio: green intensity (CellRox-positive cells) / number of nuclei (Hoechst-positive nuclei). The analysis was performed in three independent experiments (n = 12).

sec.title: Analysis of sarcomeric organization by ɑ-actinin and c-troponin staining
sec.p: The myofilament structure was visualized by immunofluorescence staining for α-actinin and c-troponin (cTnT). After treatment, iCell-CMs were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde solution (PFA) (Sigma-Aldrich) at room temperature (RT) for 15 min, washed three times with PBS, permeabilized with 0.1% Triton X-100 (Sigma-Aldrich) for 15 min at RT, and blocked with BSA 5% in PBS1x/Tween 0.1% (blocking solution) for 30 min. For ɑ-actinin staining, cells were then incubated O.N. at 4 °C with the mouse monoclonal primary antibody diluted 1:400 in blocking solution. cTnT staining was performed using rabbit polyclonal primary diluted 1:400 and incubated for 1 h at RT. Cells were subsequently washed three times in PBS, and incubated for 1 h at RT with an appropriate secondary antibody (1:400 in blocking solution). Nuclei were stained with 1 µg/ml of Hoechst 33258. Images were captured using a Nikon Eclipse Ti fluorescence microscope equipped with the Neo 5.5 sCMOS camera (Andor Technology) and NIS-Elements software (version 5.30.00 Nikon). The intensity profile of α-actinin staining was analyzed using NIS-Elements software by measuring fluorescence along sarcomeric structures in selected cardiomyocyte regions of interest. The percentage of cells with sarcomeric disorganization was evaluated as the number of cells with α-actinin disorganization / total number of cells in a blinded fashion by two independent observers on at least 100 cells per condition in three independent experiments (n = 12).

sec.title: MEA analysis
sec.p: For electrophysiological studies using the Maestro Pro MEA system (Axion Biosystems), iCell-CMs were processed as previously described. Four weeks after plating, a complete CMM change was made. MEA activity was recorded before treatment (baseline), and every 3 h for the first 24 h post-treatment, and then every 24 h up to 7d of treatment. All recordings were captured using the Axis Navigator software version 3.12.7 (Axion Biosystems) by using standard cardiac settings, at 37 °C and CO2 5%. Field Potential Duration (FPD), FPD corrected using Fredericia’s rate correction algorithm (FPDc, ms), beat period (BP, s), Spike Amplitude (mV), and Conduction Velocity (mm/ms) were analyzed using the Cardiomyocyte Analysis Tool software version 2.2.7 and AxIS Metric Plotting Tool version 2.2.5 (Axion Biosystem). For FPDc, BP, and Spike Amplitude analysis, data were expressed as the percentage of change from baseline, calculated as mean ± SEM for each treatment. Conduction Velocity has been measured as the speed of depolarization spike propagation across the culture, measured in the active electrodes (Axion Navigator software version 3.12.7, Axion Biosystems). Viability will be acquired at the start of each MEA activity recording by using the MEA Viability Software Module (Axion Biosystem) that measures impedance and MEA data from the same electrodes. Cell-electrode resistance value is measured on active electrodes and expressed as Weighted Mean Resistance (kΩ).

Four wells for each condition were analyzed in a total of five experiments (n = 20 for FP analysis and n = 9 for impedance analysis). A cut-off value of 20% FPDc variation was chosen as indicative of a significant electrophysiological effect45,46.

The local extracellular action potential (LEAP) induction experiments were performed to measure the 90% Action Potential Duration (APD90). LEAP signals were induced in iCell cardiomyocytes 72 h after DOX (0.3 µM) and BAI (1, 10, and 25 µM) and vehicles (H2O and DMSO) treatments and then recorded for 3 min. In each well, all electrodes were used for LEAP induction. APD90 (ms) was analyzed using the Cardiomyocyte Analysis Tool software version 2.2.7 and AxIS Metric Plotting Tool version 2.2.5 (Axion Biosystem). For LEAP analysis, data were obtained from two independent experiments performed in quadruplicate (n = 8).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Data are presented as mean value ± SEM. Data from multiple independent groups of samples (control, DOX-alone, DOX plus BAI 1 µM, DOX plus BAI 10, and DOX plus BAI 25 µM) were compared using two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test, using GraphPad Prism software (version 10.6.0). The statistical significance was accepted for p < 0.01.
